The Commercial System: What It Is, and Why Most Firms Run Without One

The Commercial SystemPart 1

By lowob · 2 July 2026 · 10-minute read · Strategy

A commercial system is the connected set of choices, definitions, records and routines by which a firm decides whom to serve, creates demand, reaches buyers and wins and keeps revenue. We split it into four parts: Strategy, Growth, Distribution and Revenue. Most firms run all four as activity rather than as a system, with separate definitions and tools, and the money is lost at the seams. The commercial system is also what The Build Order's brain runs on: the brain starts at the commercial line because decisions there are frequent and quickly graded, but it can only learn from a system that has agreed what its words mean.

Ask the head of marketing, the head of sales and the finance director at a 100-person firm what a qualified opportunity is. In most firms the answers differ, and the board pack, the pipeline review and the campaign report end up describing different businesses.

That gap is the subject of this series. The Build Order set out how to build a company's brain. The Commercial System is its companion: it covers what the brain operates on.

Most firms have commercial activity, not a commercial system

Activity can look like a system from inside. There is a CRM, a marketing calendar, a partner list, a pipeline meeting and a pricing sheet. Each works. None was designed with the others in mind.

The problem is old. In 2006 Philip Kotler, Neil Rackham and Suj Krishnaswamy described the tension between sales and marketing in Harvard Business Review as both economic, because the two share a budget, and cultural, because they attract different people with different working habits. Fifteen years later, Gartner's 2021 research on revenue operations made the same point in operational terms: functional silos that hand clients from department to department, each with separate technology, people and processes, are a barrier to revenue growth. Gartner predicted that 75% of the highest-growth companies would deploy a revenue operations model by 2025.

Revenue operations is part of the answer. Forrester defines it as an iterative commercial execution strategy that unifies data, processes, technology and talent across the customer lifecycle. A commercial system starts earlier, with the choices the plumbing serves: market, buyer, position, channel and price. Most companies have a list of tactics rather than a commercial thesis, and the problem is coherence, not effort (GTM strategy vs tactics).

The four parts, and the decisions each owns

We divide the commercial system into four parts. The division follows decisions, not departments. A firm of 30 people may have one person making decisions in all four.

PartThe question it answersMain recurring decisionsWhat it should leave on recordHow it is graded
StrategyWhere do we compete, and on what terms?Segment, ideal customer, position, price architecture, account prioritiesThe chosen segment and its disqualifiers, the position, the price rulesWin rate and margin in the chosen segment over two to four quarters
GrowthHow do the right buyers come to know and prefer us?Campaign spend, content priorities, tests, brand investmentEach test with its hypothesis, budget and resultQualified pipeline created, cost per qualified opportunity
DistributionThrough whom and where do we reach buyers?Partner selection, channel terms, events, marketplacesEach partner or channel with its expected and actual contributionPartner-sourced and partner-influenced revenue, channel cost
RevenueHow do we win, price and keep the deal?Qualification, discount exceptions, proposals, forecast calls, renewalsEvery exception and loss with a reason and an ownerForecast accuracy, realised price, retention

Two features matter more than the rows. Each part produces something another consumes: Strategy produces the ideal customer profile that Growth targets and Revenue qualifies against (How to write an ICP), and Revenue produces the loss reasons that should change Strategy's position. And every part has decisions that recur, which is what makes the commercial line the right place for a learning system to start.

Why the system has become harder to run

McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers found buyers used an average of ten interaction channels, up from five in 2016, and more than half would likely switch supplier after a poor experience across channels. Each channel creates records in a different tool.

The buying group has grown too. Forrester's 2024 State of Business Buying study, drawing on more than 16,000 global business buyers, found 13 people involved in the average purchase decision, with 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. Nearly all purchases, 91%, stalled at some point.

Buyers also spend little of that time with suppliers. Gartner's 2018 survey of 750 B2B buyers in complex purchases found they spent 17% of their buying time meeting potential suppliers, shared across every supplier considered. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase.

A buyer who meets the firm through a partner, a webinar, a search result and a seller will notice if the four describe different offers. A commercial system is how a firm makes sure they do not.

Where the four parts break: the seams

Marketing usually runs campaigns competently, and sales usually runs deals competently. The money leaks where one part hands to another.

SeamWhat should pass across itWhat usually passes instead
Strategy to GrowthA named segment with disqualifiersA broad description and a list of job titles
Growth to RevenueOpportunities with a buying group attachedIndividual leads, scored on activity
Distribution to RevenuePartner-sourced deals, tagged at creationDeals whose source is argued about at commission time
Revenue to StrategyLoss reasons and price exceptions, with patternsA closed-lost stage with no reason recorded

The Growth-to-Revenue seam is the best documented. Forrester research cited in its 2023 analysis of marketing-qualified leads found fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, partly because several leads contribute to one opportunity and attributing a deal to any one of them is meaningless. Firms that pass buying groups rather than leads do better: Forrester found clients who delivered three or more buying-group members to sales saw a 50% increase in conversion from meeting to closed-won.

The Revenue-to-Strategy seam is the least visible. Without recorded loss reasons, positioning and pricing follow the loudest anecdote. Validity's 2025 survey of 602 CRM users found 37% reported revenue lost as a direct result of poor data quality, and 76% said less than half of their organisation's CRM data was accurate and complete.

The losses rarely sit inside a function. They sit where one function hands to another.

How the commercial system relates to The Build Order

The Build Order argued that the brain should start at the commercial line (Why the brain starts at the commercial line), because decisions that are frequent, similar, quickly graded and defended are where a decision system learns first. Almost every recurring decision in the four-part table passes that test. The commercial system supplies the definitions and decisions; The Build Order supplies the layers that store, connect, record and learn from them.

Commercial system elementBuild Order layerWhat breaks if it is missing
Agreed definitions: segment, qualified opportunity, stage, loss reasonRules the store followsThe CRM holds data nobody can compare
Systems of record for accounts, deals, partners and campaignsStoreContext is spread across inboxes and memory
Shared view of each account across the four partsContext layerEach function sees a fragment of the buyer
Recorded decisions: segment choice, price exceptions, partner terms, forecast callsDecision recordOutcomes cannot be traced to the judgment that caused them
Operating rhythm that reviews outcomesLearningThe firm repeats its errors at the same cadence

The order matters. A brain wired onto a commercial line with no shared definitions will reason fluently over inconsistent data. Our explainer sets out the components in more detail (What is a commercial operating system?), and Part 9 of The Build Order lists the decisions worth recording first (The ten commercial decisions worth recording).

This series takes the four parts in order. Parts 2 to 6 cover Strategy: positioning, segment selection, pricing architecture, market maps and the operating rhythm that holds the system together.

Building one without a reorganisation

A commercial system does not require a new department. In firms of 20 to 500 people it usually requires four things, most of which cost time rather than money.

One accountable owner. Someone must own the seams, not just the parts: often the founder in a small firm, a revenue operations lead in a larger one. Specialists without a single named owner of the commercial problem become a roster (The modular GTM team).

One set of definitions. Segment, qualified opportunity, stage entry criteria, partner-sourced, loss reasons. Agreed once, changed only by a recorded decision.

One record of decisions. Recurring commercial decisions, written with a reason, an owner, a status and an expected outcome.

One rhythm. A weekly, monthly and quarterly cadence in which the four parts read the same numbers. Part 6 covers it.

A 20-person firm can run all of this in a shared document and a weekly meeting; a 200-person firm needs it in the CRM (The scale ladder).

Illustrative example: one definition of a qualified opportunity
Decision
Replace three competing definitions of a qualified opportunity (marketing's, sales' and the partner team's) with one, tied to the ideal customer profile and a named buying-group contact.
Reason and owner
Board reports and pipeline reviews showed pipeline figures that differed by more than a third depending on who prepared them. Agreed by the leadership team; owned by the commercial lead.
What changed
Marketing reports opportunities, not leads; partner deals are tagged at creation; the definition is reviewed quarterly and any change is recorded with its reason.

Illustrative: a composite of a 70-person emerging technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Design the seams, not just the parts. Most commercial losses happen where one function hands work to another.
  • Divide by decision, not department. Strategy, Growth, Distribution and Revenue each own recurring decisions that can be recorded and graded.
  • Agree the words before wiring the tools. A brain built on inconsistent definitions reasons well over bad inputs.
  • Start small and on the record. One owner, one set of definitions, one decision record and one rhythm is enough to begin.
Gateway card

Before you call it a commercial system

  • One named owner for the seams between the four parts
  • Written definitions for segment, qualified opportunity, stage and loss reason
  • Partner and channel source captured when a deal is created
  • A required loss reason on every closed-lost deal
  • A weekly, monthly and quarterly review that uses the same numbers

Common questions

What is a commercial system in business?

It is the connected set of choices, definitions, records and routines a firm uses to decide whom to serve, create demand, reach buyers and win and keep revenue. We divide it into Strategy, Growth, Distribution and Revenue.

What is the difference between a commercial system and revenue operations?

Revenue operations unifies the data, processes, technology and people behind revenue. A commercial system includes that, plus the strategic choices it serves: segment, position, channel and price.

Why do sales and marketing disagree on pipeline numbers?

Usually because each uses its own definition of a qualified opportunity. One written definition, changed only on the record, removes most of the disagreement.

Where should a company start building its commercial system?

With definitions: agree what a qualified opportunity and a loss reason are, then record the recurring decisions that depend on them.
